title: Chapter One: The Lamp at the End of the Lane

blocks.c: Chapter One: The Lamp at the End of the Lane

The last lamp on Weatherbell Lane had been out for eleven days, and Ines had counted every one of them on the inside of her wrist, in ink, the way her grandmother had taught her to count anything that mattered. Eleven strokes, four of them smudged by rain. The lamp itself stood at the turn where the cobbles gave up and the road became mud with opinions about it.

She had been told, twice, that the lane was not on her round. She had been told once more, with feeling, that a lamp nobody walked under was a lamp nobody needed. Ines had nodded at all three tellings and had come anyway, because the ledger in the guildhall listed the lamp as lit, and Ines had a great and unfashionable respect for ledgers.
The ladder was where she had left it. So was the wind.

At the top of the ladder the world went quiet in the way high places do. The glass housing was clouded with a winter's worth of soot, and inside it the wick sat curled and black, like something asleep and unwilling to discuss the matter.

Ines cleaned the glass first. That was the order: glass, reservoir, wick, flame. Her grandmother had been fond of saying that a lamplighter who lights before she cleans is only making a brighter mess, and had been fonder still of saying it twice.
Light is not a thing you carry to a place. It is a thing a place agrees to keep, if you have asked it properly.

The wick caught on the third strike. It burned yellow, then white, then settled into the steady amber that meant the oil was good and the housing was sealed, and Ines allowed herself, for four full seconds, to be pleased.
Then she looked down the lane and saw that the mud held footprints, and that the footprints had been made by someone walking towards the dark on purpose.
